section_summary: This section documents mounting American public and congressional pressure to halt oil, scrap-metal, and other strategic exports to Japan, together with State Department replies explaining the export-licensing system and its national-defense rationale. It also contains diplomatic and intelligence reporting on Japanese acquisition of aluminum tanks, scrap iron, petroleum, rubber, tin, copra, and other commodities from Mexico, Ecuador, the Netherlands East Indies, Malaya, and the Philippines. The final portion examines Japan’s dependence on imported iron ore, pig iron, and scrap, and debates whether restricting Philippine and Malayan iron-ore exports would materially weaken Japanese steel production without causing disproportionate local economic harm.

subfiles.title: Continuation of Paine College letter protesting strategic exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The writer questions why the United States aids Britain while continuing to send oil and other supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The surviving final page argues that recent exports to Japan had risen sharply and calls the policy contradictory. The writer asks when the United States will cease helping Japan prosecute its aggression and requests public clarification rather than a personal reply.

subfiles.title: Shanley transmittal and routing sheet for the Bennett letter
subfiles.about: Congressman Shanley forwards a constituent letter concerning exports to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: The page is largely a congressional letterhead and departmental routing record. Later correspondence identifies it as Shanley’s transmittal of R. J. Bennett’s protest about shipments of strategic material.

subfiles.title: R. J. Bennett on scrap, oil, and machine-tool exports
subfiles.about: Bennett contrasts a government request for transit-industry scrap with continued strategic exports to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: Bennett quotes an American Transit Association request for information about scrap that could be made available to the government. He asks why scrap iron, oil, machine tools, and similar materials have continued to strengthen countries he regards as enemies.

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledgment to James A. Shanley
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges receipt of Shanley’s transmittal of the Bennett letter.
subfiles.summary: Hull identifies Bennett as vice president of The Connecticut Company and notes that his letter concerns shipments to Japan and the Soviet Union. He promises prompt attention to Shanley’s request.

subfiles.title: Welles reply to Shanley on export controls
subfiles.about: Welles explains the licensing controls governing scrap iron, petroleum products, and machine tools exported to Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that a long list of strategic articles may be exported only under license. Applications are reviewed for their possible effect on national defense, and both the controlled list and licensing policy are continually adjusted as conditions change. Bennett’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Daniels despatch on aluminum tanks shipped from Manzanillo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports how aluminum tanks covered by a Mexican export prohibition nevertheless left Manzanillo for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy confirms that the tanks were loaded aboard a Japanese ship despite a special instruction to Mexican customs authorities. The Ministry of Finance explained that customs had authorized aluminum sheets or plates without realizing that the cargo consisted of the prohibited tanks. The report clears La Consolidada of involvement and says an agent of A. Z. Phillips arranged the purchase.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution of the Daniels despatch
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The Department circulates the Mexico Embassy’s report on aluminum tanks shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum transmits a copy of confidential despatch no. 13016 for possible intelligence value. It identifies A. Z. Phillips and Manzanillo in the subject line.

subfiles.title: Guayaquil report on scrap-iron exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The consul reports plans by T. Sato & Cia. to ship recurring lots of Ecuadorian scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: An initial 100-ton shipment was expected aboard the Norway Maru, with similar monthly shipments planned for at least three more months. The despatch gives the local price and explains that the scrap was being collected around Guayaquil and stored beside the Guayas River.

subfiles.title: Cosgrave’s correspondence fragment
subfiles.about: The surviving page records a San Francisco business correspondent and State Department file number but preserves no substantive message.
subfiles.summary: Only the Cosgrave’s letterhead, General Manager’s office, a June 1941 date, and filing annotations remain legible. The subject matter cannot be recovered from this page.

subfiles.title: Fred A. Smith protests exports from the Pacific coast
subfiles.about: Smith condemns shipments of scrap iron, copper, gasoline, and wheat that he believes strengthen Japan and Germany.
subfiles.summary: Smith says residents of the Washington coast are bewildered by strategic exports to Japan while the administration promotes aid to Britain. He also alleges that Canadian wheat shipped to Vladivostok on Japanese vessels may ultimately feed German soldiers. He characterizes the trade as unpatriotic profiteering.

subfiles.title: Charles J. Turck asks for action on oil shipments
subfiles.about: Turck asks the administration to answer press allegations that American and British commercial interests continue supplying Japan with oil.
subfiles.summary: Turck argues that continued oil traffic aids Japan’s war against China and resembles the appeasement policy condemned elsewhere. He says the allegations must be answered by immediate action and asks for an explanation.

subfiles.title: Allen reply to Turck on petroleum licensing
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department outlines the petroleum export restrictions in force since July 1940.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that high-octane aviation fuel and aviation lubricants were initially restricted outside the Western Hemisphere and British Empire and that licensing was later extended to other petroleum products. It says licenses are refused when a shipment would harm national defense and emphasizes that controls are continually revised.

subfiles.title: Peter V. Ross urges an end to oil shipments
subfiles.about: Ross conveys Pacific-coast concern about increasing oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ross says the public cannot understand why shipments of vital war material continue to increase. He praises Hull’s conduct of other foreign affairs and urges him to stop the flow of oil to East Asia.

subfiles.title: William Lewis Gerstle requests an oil embargo
subfiles.about: Gerstle asks for an embargo on oil and gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Writing from San Francisco, Gerstle argues that the shipments materially assist Japan’s war of aggression against China. He asks that the government give serious consideration to imposing an embargo.

subfiles.title: Senator Brown forwards the Garner letter
subfiles.about: Brown forwards William A. Garner’s constituent letter and requests information for a reply.
subfiles.summary: The senator describes Garner’s letter as self-explanatory and asks the Secretary of State to return it with relevant information. Departmental annotations record its receipt and routing.

subfiles.title: William A. Garner condemns gasoline sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Garner attacks the sale of gasoline to Japan while Americans face taxes, higher prices, and a possible domestic shortage.
subfiles.summary: Garner calls it disgraceful to supply fuel for Japanese tanks and aircraft used against China. He warns that the governing party will suffer politically if officials permit the trade and asks whether major oil companies are also supplying Hitler. The letter also discusses defense taxes, labor unrest, and public dissatisfaction.

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledgment to Senator Brown
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Brown’s transmittal of Garner’s letter about oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The brief reply records the subject and promises prompt attention. It is an interim acknowledgment preceding the substantive response.

subfiles.title: Welles reply to Brown on petroleum export controls
subfiles.about: Welles explains the statutory licensing system governing petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply reviews restrictions begun in July 1940 on aviation fuel and lubricants and subsequently extended to other petroleum products. It states that proposed exports are evaluated for their effect on national defense and that controls are adjusted as conditions change. Garner’s letter and an accompanying newspaper clipping are returned.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs summary of Tokyo despatch on Netherlands East Indies exports
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Dutch plans to limit strategic exports to Japan to estimated domestic requirements.
subfiles.summary: It reviews proposed Japanese quotas for rubber, tin, and copra and notes concern that excess imports might be re-exported to Germany. The Netherlands East Indies and Malayan authorities were coordinating treatment of Japanese orders. The memorandum concludes that the subject is mainly of reference value after negotiations were broken off.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch no. 5588 on Netherlands East Indies exports
subfiles.about: Grew transmits Dutch data and proposed quotas for commodities exported from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Based on information from W. H. De Roos, the despatch compares Japanese requirements and recent purchases of rubber, tin, copra, coconut oil, palm products, castor oil, rope fibers, pepper, tobacco, tea, and sugar. It describes unusually large Japanese demands and Dutch-Malayan coordination intended to prevent stockpiling or re-export to Germany. Detailed historical production, import, and quota figures are supplied for the principal commodities.

subfiles.title: Greenwich Council of Women protests Standard Oil sales
subfiles.from: Mrs. Stanley P. Woodard, Greenwich Council of Women
subfiles.about: The council condemns Standard Oil of New Jersey for supplying Japan with oil used in the war in China.
subfiles.summary: Woodard calls the company’s public explanations weak and morally irresponsible. She argues that Americans do not wish to bear the historical stigma of enabling Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Senator Byrd forwards the Holloway letter
subfiles.about: Byrd forwards R. C. Holloway’s complaint about oil shipments to Japan and requests the Department’s comments.
subfiles.summary: The senator briefly identifies the constituent and subject. He asks Hull for comments that will permit a response to Holloway.

subfiles.title: R. C. Holloway objects to oil exports amid threatened shortages
subfiles.about: Holloway protests sending oil and iron to Japan while eastern consumers face gasoline and heating-oil restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Holloway says he would accept limited automobile use but fears a shortage could make his oil-heating system unusable. He sees a contradiction between assisting China and permitting Japan to acquire the resources used against it. He asks Byrd to protect his interests.

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledgment to Senator Byrd
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Byrd’s transmittal of Holloway’s letter about oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department records receipt of Byrd’s inquiry and promises prompt attention. The message serves as an interim response.

subfiles.title: Welles reply to Byrd on export and domestic petroleum policy
subfiles.about: Welles explains petroleum licensing and distinguishes Atlantic transportation shortages from Pacific export movements.
subfiles.summary: The reply says petroleum exports have long required licenses and that controls were tightened further on June 20. It assures Byrd that eastern consumer needs will be considered, while explaining that the threatened shortage is fundamentally a transportation problem and does not directly concern Pacific shipments in foreign vessels. Holloway’s letter and newspaper clipping are returned.

subfiles.title: Bureau of the Budget request for views on H.J. Res. 189
subfiles.from: Frederick J. Bailey, Bureau of the Budget
subfiles.about: The Budget Bureau asks for State Department views on legislation mandating an end to petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The proposed resolution would invoke section 6 of Public No. 703 to prohibit further petroleum shipments to Japan. The letter encloses a proposed War Department report and requests a foreign-policy assessment before the Budget Bureau replies.

subfiles.title: War Department draft report opposing H.J. Res. 189
subfiles.about: The War Department recommends against legislation automatically prohibiting petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The draft acknowledges petroleum as a vital defense resource but warns that country-specific restrictions could have far-reaching international consequences. It argues that changing world conditions require continued presidential discretion rather than a statutory mandate. The report therefore recommends that H.J. Res. 189 not be enacted.

subfiles.title: Welles reply to the Budget Bureau on H.J. Res. 189
subfiles.about: Welles strongly opposes enactment of the proposed statutory petroleum embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: From the standpoint of foreign policy, Welles concurs with the reasoning of the proposed War Department report. He urges that Congress not enact H.J. Res. 189 and thereby restrict executive discretion.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on Japanese reaction to prospective oil restrictions
subfiles.about: Grew reports Japanese press reaction to possible restrictions on military exports from the eastern United States.
subfiles.summary: The Japan Times and Advertiser reported suspicion in Japanese industrial circles that an oil embargo might be intended to provoke friction with the United States. The Nichi Nichi also carried a report of President Roosevelt’s remarks about possible action against Italian and Japanese consulates. The telegram was sent through Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Asano Bussan appeal concerning lubricating oil aboard the Azuma Maru
subfiles.about: Asano Bussan seeks permission to load 904 barrels of low-grade lubricating oil at Philadelphia.
subfiles.summary: The company states that the oil was purchased from Sinclair Refining and prepared specifically for shipment. It supplies technical specifications and argues that the grades require no export license, are not important to national defense, and are not in short supply. Asano asks that the planned shipment be allowed to proceed.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Japanese officials about blocked oil shipments
subfiles.about: Japanese Embassy officials ask the Department to reconsider the stoppage of lubricating-oil shipments from Atlantic ports.
subfiles.summary: Sadao Iguchi and Mr. Inouye presented Asano Bussan’s memorandum concerning the Azuma Maru shipment at Philadelphia. Mr. Coville requested information about outstanding contracts and said the Embassy should supply a written statement of the considerations it wanted reviewed. The parties agreed that no action would be expected until that memorandum arrived.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Asano Bussan
subfiles.from: Harold W. Moseley, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Asano’s oil-shipment appeal and sends the applicable export-control materials.
subfiles.summary: The brief response encloses Press Release no. 309 and Export Control Schedule no. 10. It does not grant the requested permission directly.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy memorandum on the Azuma Maru shipment
subfiles.about: The Embassy requests relief for the stopped Azuma Maru oil cargo and for similar contracts concluded before June 16.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy argues that the low-grade oil legally required no license and that sudden intervention would cause losses to American and Japanese firms engaged in bona fide trade. It asks for special consideration of completed contracts and measures to ensure smoother future trade between Japan and the United States.

subfiles.title: Draft response explaining Atlantic-coast petroleum restrictions
subfiles.about: The Department attributes the Atlantic export restrictions to a threatened petroleum shortage in the eastern United States.
subfiles.summary: The draft says a comprehensive survey by the Petroleum Coordinator for National Defense disclosed a potentially critical shortage. It explains that restrictions on eastern-seaboard exports were therefore necessary to protect regional supply.

subfiles.title: Revised response to the Japanese Embassy on petroleum exports
subfiles.about: A revised memorandum explains the regional petroleum shortage and the geographic scope of export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum repeats that a survey revealed a threatened critical shortage in the eastern United States. Restrictions were imposed on petroleum exports from the Atlantic seaboard, while shipments from other ports, including the Gulf and Pacific coasts, could proceed under existing arrangements.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Controls memorandum on Philippine iron-ore policy
subfiles.about: The memorandum records consultations over a Philippine iron-ore quota and the need to coordinate with the British.
subfiles.summary: The difficult handwriting indicates that Controls discussed the Philippine iron-ore question with Far Eastern Affairs, including Mr. Adams. Officials were not ready to recommend a quota until the outcome of negotiations with the British was clearer. The note suggests that Far Eastern Affairs continue the matter with British representatives.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note on Philippine iron-ore shipments
subfiles.about: The note reviews Philippine iron-ore export quantities and recent instructions concerning shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum compares normal annual Philippine shipments with the high level reached in 1940 and shipments during the first months of 1941. It refers to a telegram sent to the Philippine administration and asks how the broader quota question should be handled.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs routing note on an iron-ore directive
subfiles.to: Division of Controls and Dean Acheson
subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs urges prompt issuance of the directive discussed in Adams’s attached memorandum.
subfiles.summary: The note refers specifically to the final paragraph of Adams’s memorandum. It argues that early issuance would improve the situation from a psychological standpoint.

subfiles.title: Adams memorandum on Philippine iron-ore exports
subfiles.from: Mr. Adams, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Adams evaluates the temporary authorization of unrestricted Philippine iron-ore exports and recommends an eventual prewar-level quota.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports that Philippine shipments to Japan had risen from a normal 600,000 tons to about 1,220,000 tons in 1940 and were still increasing in early 1941. It argues that an immediate prohibition would leave ore stranded, cause unemployment, and have limited effect because shipping capacity already constrained deliveries. A forthcoming directive was expected to permit normal prewar quantities.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter enclosing iron-and-steel studies
subfiles.about: The British Embassy sends studies comparing the importance of Malayan and Philippine iron-ore exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer recalls an agreement with General Maxwell to discuss the matter with Colonel Burr. Copies of a memorandum and statistical tables already supplied to Burr are enclosed for Acheson’s information.

subfiles.title: The Supply Position in the Iron and Steel Industry in Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum analyzes Japan’s iron-and-steel capacity and dependence on imported ore, pig iron, and scrap.
subfiles.summary: It argues that Japanese steel output had plateaued because domestic ore and pig-iron production could not keep pace with capacity. Japan’s industry had developed around imported scrap and remained vulnerable to the loss of foreign ore, pig iron, and scrap. The paper reviews production plans, the limited success of low-grade ore development in Japan and Korea, and the possibility that Japan had accumulated a scrap reserve by 1939.

subfiles.title: Iron Ore Exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses whether Malayan and Philippine iron-ore exports should be curtailed.
subfiles.summary: It estimates that embargoes on scrap and reduced pig-iron exports had already cut Japan’s raw-material supply substantially. A 50 percent reduction in Malayan and Philippine ore would yield only a further limited reduction while risking economic disruption, especially in Terengganu. The paper recommends concentrating instead on manganese, chrome, tungsten, vanadium, nickel, cobalt, and molybdenum, which were more directly important to armaments.

subfiles.title: Statistical appendices on Japanese iron and steel raw materials
subfiles.about: The appendices quantify Japanese iron-ore imports, domestic ore production, pig-iron output, scrap requirements, and foreign-source dependence.
subfiles.summary: Tables compare ore imported from British Malaya, the Philippines, Australia, and other sources with Japanese domestic production and pig-iron output. Further tables estimate raw-material needs for steelmaking and reported scrap consumption and imports. A final table expresses major foreign sources as percentages of Japan’s total iron-and-steel raw-material supply.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs review of the British iron-ore memorandum
subfiles.from: Edwin O. Reischauer, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews British arguments against reducing Malayan iron-ore exports and records the differing view of the Office of Philippine Affairs.
subfiles.summary: The British analysis claimed that a large cut in Malayan and Philippine shipments would reduce Japan’s total raw-material supply only modestly and would harm Terengganu’s economy. Philippine Affairs recalculated the effect as larger once U.S. scrap exports were eliminated and argued that returning shipments to 1938 levels would not cause serious dislocation. A Singapore freezing order was expected to eliminate trade with the Japanese Empire, and the memorandum concludes that no further action appeared necessary.
